name: Hana Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, government or campaigners. We keep your answers confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead eight people in the ordering office of a large packaging company. I check late shipments, settle disputes between sales and the warehouse, and tell my team which customer needs a call before lunch. I finished an MBA, but this is still a job where remembering who made a promise matters more than a slide deck. I have never used an AI tool myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part do you enjoy, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a frightened new hire steady enough to speak to a difficult customer. The pay is low for a team lead, and rent and the loan for my MBA leave less than a month of expenses in the bank. There aren’t many management openings near my mother, and I’m not eager to start somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team the AI Plateau is another office gadget, and we still have to answer for a missed delivery. I wouldn’t call it a threat at the morning meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, routine checks are part of why our office needs eight people. My own job feels safe for now, but I fear the company might use even small savings to leave a vacancy open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll keep the dispatch meeting and the weekly customer calls as they are in 2026. If the small tool arrives next year, I’ll ask to see its error log before signing off; I won’t put rent money into software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy rather than scared. Rent was already tight before anyone said AI, and a quiet vacancy would put more work on the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense presses first if the company freezes a post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The MBA loan payment comes straight after rent, so groceries become the adjustable line. I already buy lunch twice a week instead of every day. I wouldn’t tell the team that at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check the new tool’s mistakes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check it. A shipment marked complete can still be sitting by the loading door. My boss wants a clean dashboard, but customers remember the missing boxes. A manager still has to own that call.

say: **Customer calls** still need a person who knows the promise made.
I’d tell the team a small **AI tool** changes little in our morning routine.
think: Our eight-person office may lose a **vacancy** even if nobody is fired.
My **rent and MBA loan** already leave almost no room for a surprise.
do: **Keep** the dispatch meeting and weekly customer calls through 2026.
**Check** the tool’s error log before approving its shipment figures after launch.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordinary bills and a possible unfilled post.
S0.quote: A shipment marked complete can still be sitting by the loading door.
fieldNote: Her public **confidence** protects the team from worry, while she privately counts the effect of one unfilled post.
The **MBA loan** and rent constrain any experiment; she refuses to spend her own money on software.

steps.text: Keep the dispatch meeting and weekly customer calls on the same schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption means we have to prove why a manager is worth paying. I’d ask the team to keep notes on the customer problems the software cannot settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, writing replies, checking orders and planning shifts are most of my screen time. If those go, I may be left supervising fewer people for less pay. I’m good at a hard conversation, but a spreadsheet of savings could beat that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’ll write down the cases our team rescues and take them to my boss at the next budget meeting. As tools roll in, I’ll ask for a paid training session and attend if the company approves it before I sign off on a new workflow, and I’ll stop buying lunch out to add a little cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That makes me anxious. I can make a case for the team, but I cannot promise the company will value the cases it never sees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on that list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a hospital’s carton count was wrong, and we corrected it before their morning delivery. I would record the call, the hours saved and who noticed the mistake. My boss likes numbers more than stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You dislike new software, yet you’d take training. What’s the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll take the company-paid training if approved, after someone shows the system works. I will not spend evenings teaching myself a product so the company can delete a post. That is a business cost, not a private hobby.

say: **Managers** must show the customer problems that automation misses.
I’d ask my team to record **rescued orders**, not just completed tickets.
think: Writing, checking and **shift planning** fill much of my day.
A smaller team could mean **lower pay** despite my skill with customers.
do: **Record** rescued orders and take the numbers to the next 2026 budget meeting.
**Request** paid AI training and attend if the company approves it before the new workflow begins.
**Cut** bought lunches to build a small cushion.
feel: **Anxious** because she can make her case but cannot control the budget.
S1.quote: I will not spend evenings teaching myself a product so the company can delete a post.
fieldNote: She turns personal **resistance** into a demand for employer-paid training after proof that a tool works.
Her **customer evidence** is specific, but it may not protect her pay if headcount shrinks.

steps.text: Record rescued hospital and customer orders for the next budget meeting
Attend paid AI software training if the company approves the session
Stop buying lunch out twice a week to save cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office that AGI by 2028 needs a serious plan, not a brave speech. I’d say we owe customers a human contact while the company sorts out liability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, cheap thinking work by 2028 could take the reports, order checks and the team schedule before I can repay my MBA. Robots arriving around 2031 are beside the point for my desk. I expect the company would cut my team and perhaps my post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask my boss for a written plan for management jobs, and I’d take my loan statement to the lender to ask about a lower monthly payment. If AGI arrives in 2028, I’d apply for the remaining customer escalation roles, but there are few nearby; I would ask my mother if I could stay with her if I lost pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. I can speak steadily in front of staff, then lie awake working out which payment could wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say I might need the spare room for three months, not forever. My mother has already helped with the MBA once, so the words would stick in my throat. I would still ask before I missed rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in the written plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date for any cut, a list of posts still open to us and severance in plain numbers. I cannot make a budget from a promise to be flexible. The company should be honest with the people who trained its customers.

say: **Customers** need a human contact while the company assigns responsibility.
I’d ask for a **management plan** with dates and clear terms.
think: AGI could remove my **reports and schedules** by 2028, three years before capable robots arrive.
I expect a **team cut** that may include my own post.
do: **Ask** my boss for written job and severance terms this month.
**Contact** the MBA lender about lowering my monthly payment now.
**Apply** for customer escalation posts if AGI arrives in 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing pay before the MBA debt is cleared.
S2.quote: I cannot make a budget from a promise to be flexible.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 thinking shock** from robots expected around 2031; her desk role has little physical shelter.
The public call for **liability** masks a private request for her mother’s spare room if income stops.

steps.text: Apply for customer escalation posts in the first year after AGI arrives
Ask mother about her spare room if pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us a window to put the real customer exceptions on paper. We should ask for a place in the new organisation while there is time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough for me to clear much of the MBA loan if my job lasts. It is not long enough to pretend a manager who mainly plans and checks will stay untouched. The robots in about 2034 do not change my first problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d put a fixed extra amount toward the MBA loan each payday and ask my boss to let me spend one day a month with the customer claims team. I’d test that path for a year before applying elsewhere; once AGI arrives around 2031, I’d seek a claims role if our management layer is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, though less cornered than in the 2028 picture. Having five years gives me an order for the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you really put toward the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe forty a month if I stop taking taxis after late shifts. I would have to check the actual statement before promising even that. I am not going to claim a grand savings plan on a thin salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why customer claims?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A damaged shipment brings the customer, insurer and warehouse into one room. I’m useful when three people disagree about what happened. Software may draft the forms, but I want to see if that dispute work remains paid.

say: **Five years** lets us document customer exceptions and ask for new roles.
I’d ask for a place in the **new organisation** before cuts begin.
think: The **MBA loan** could shrink by 2031 if pay continues.
My planning and checking work remains **exposed** years before robots arrive around 2034.
do: Pay about **forty extra monthly** on the MBA loan if the budget allows.
**Shadow** the customer claims team one day a month for a year.
**Apply** for a claims post if management jobs disappear after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough time to try one careful route.
S3.quote: Software may draft the forms, but I want to see if that dispute work remains paid.
fieldNote: The extra **time** turns alarm into a limited trial, constrained by low pay and uncertain future vacancies.
She chooses **claims work** because it uses her strength in resolving disagreements, while admitting it too may change.

steps.text: Pay about forty extra each month toward the MBA loan if the budget allows
Shadow the customer claims team monthly for one year
Apply for a claims post if management roles disappear after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 is enough notice for firms to deal fairly with workers. I’d ask management to make a training and redundancy schedule now rather than springing one on us later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I could pay off the MBA and build some savings, if my salary holds. My job’s planning and checking could go when AGI arrives in 2036, and robots around 2039 are a later problem for the warehouse. I might be able to lead a service team, but I cannot count on that post existing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’ll pay the loan on time and keep leading the eight-person team. I’ll ask the company for a two-year development path into customer disputes, then review the openings every six months. In the first year after 2036, I’d take an offered service lead post if one exists, or look outside the town if it does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy. Ten years gives me a chance to move, but the promise depends on pay and real openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move away from your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try to avoid it because my mother lives alone and I visit each Sunday. If the only paid management role were elsewhere, I would travel first and decide after three months. I will not announce a move before seeing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fair notice look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written timetable, paid time to train and a real answer about severance. I would accept a tough business decision more readily than a surprise meeting. People should not have to guess for ten years.

say: **Ten years** gives firms time to publish training and redundancy plans.
I’d ask for **paid training** before any management posts end.
think: I could clear my **MBA debt** and save if wages continue.
A future **service lead** opening is possible, not guaranteed.
do: **Lead** the eight-person team and pay the loan on time in 2026.
**Request** a two-year path into customer disputes and review openings twice yearly.
**Travel** for an outside post after 2036 only if a real offer appears.
feel: **Uneasy** because pay and vacancies must hold for the plan to work.
S4.quote: People should not have to guess for ten years.
fieldNote: Her long-horizon plan remains **conditional** on salary, openings and an actual offer outside town.
Her **mother’s needs** make an outside job a three-month travel trial before she decides about moving.

steps.text: Lead the ordering team and keep paying the MBA loan on time
Review service lead openings every six months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my office work could vanish before I clear the loan. A written schedule for cuts, paid training and a real severance figure would let me plan. My mother’s spare room is a last resort, not a plan I want to make for her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is expected to explain a wrong order to a customer after a machine approves it. I can take responsibility for a decision I made. I will not sign my name to a number nobody checked.

headlineQuote: I will not sign my name to a number nobody checked.
portrait: **Hana, 27**, is an MBA-trained team lead managing eight people in a large packaging company’s ordering office.
Her **low pay**, rent and MBA loan leave less than one month of expenses saved and few nearby management alternatives.
She has never used **AI tools** and will attend company-paid training only if approved after seeing the system work.
She moves from **unease** in AI Plateau to alarm by 2028, then makes conditional debt and claims plans with more notice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her desk work before she repays the MBA loan.
whatWouldHelp: A written **cut timetable**, paid training and a real severance figure would let her plan.
